correctness.rationale: Choose countably many distinct coordinates and slices forcing the selected coordinate norm above \(1-1/K\). For arbitrary selected points, the average of the off-coordinate remainders is at most \((p/K)^{1/p}\), while the average of the disjoint coordinate pieces is at most \(K^{1/p-1}\); both tend to zero, so the chosen countable slice family determines the origin even though points may have arbitrary support elsewhere. For uniqueness, regroup around any coordinate and apply Proposition 3.11 of Langemets--Lõo--Martín--Rueda Zoca, which forces the Daugavet coordinate of every SCD point to vanish.
correctness.risk: The endpoints \(p=1,\infty\) are excluded and the source explicitly records failure of the analogous existence statement in Daugavet examples there.

value.rationale: The result shows a genuinely nonseparable phenomenon: a unit ball of arbitrarily large density has a single point determined by only countably many slices, while every coordinate space can itself have no SCD points. Removing countability from the index set is a natural structural extension of the paper's direct-sum theory.
value.risk: The proof is elementary once the countable construction and two-summand obstruction are known, so the contribution is a focused cardinality extension rather than a new technique.

final_claim: For any infinite index set \(\Gamma\) and \(1<p<\infty\), the origin is an SCD point of the unit ball of every nontrivial arbitrary-index \(\ell_p\)-sum; if every coordinate space has the Daugavet property then the origin is the unique SCD point.
limitations: The result requires \(1<p<\infty\) and nontrivial coordinate spaces.
No claim is made that arbitrary-index direct sums are SCD sets.
